results.result: The automated touchscreen testing system substantially reduces testing time (by up to 10 times) and increases throughput (approximately 10 times higher) compared to conventional touchscreen testing methods, with animals completing multiple sessions per day without experimenter involvement.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C9, C45, C68-C69 collectively demonstrate the automated system's performance advantages. The comparison to conventional methods (Milton et al., 2021) is explicitly stated with quantitative metrics (5-10x faster, 10x throughput), and data in Figure 2A supports these findings. The mechanism (self-directed sessions, no experimenter involvement) is clearly described.

results.result: Serial reversals were progressively easier to learn than the initial reversal, with fewer sessions required to reach performance criterion, driven largely by reduced omissions at the second and third reversals.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 are supported by statistical analysis (p-values provided) and data in Figures 2B, 2D-E. This demonstrates the expected learning effect across serial reversals and validates the task's sensitivity to learning improvements.

results.result: Restricting touchscreen access to the dark phase increased accuracy overall and reduced omitted responses during initial stages of discrimination and reversal learning, consistent with increased activity and attention during the dark period in rats.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49, C70 are supported by statistical comparisons (p-values provided) and data in Figures 2G-K. The finding is contextualized with citations to established knowledge about circadian activity patterns (Milton et al., 2021; Bruinsma et al., 2019), strengthening the interpretation.

results.result: Contrary to expectations, cognitive inflexibility measured by reversal learning does not predispose rats to pathological weight loss in ABA. Instead, rats predisposed to weight loss (ABA-susceptible) were more quickly able to learn the reversal task prior to ABA exposure than ABA-resistant rats.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11, C74-C75 represent a major finding contradicting the authors' hypothesis. The result is supported by data in Figure 3 showing ABA-resistant rats required significantly more sessions at first reversal (p=0.0142) and more non-correct responses (p=0.0401). Statistical analysis is appropriate, though the lack of significant difference in total trials (p=0.1132) introduces some complexity.

results.result: Rats that went on to be susceptible versus resistant to ABA learned pairwise discrimination at the same rate, but resistant rats required significantly more sessions at the first reversal to reach performance criterion, with increased non-correct responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52, C78 are supported by statistical analysis and data in Figures 3B-F. The finding that susceptible rats showed better reversal learning (faster adaptation) is counterintuitive but well-documented with appropriate statistics and multiple measures (sessions, non-correct responses, learning curves).

results.result: During initial discrimination learning, rats that went on to be resistant to ABA spent more time engaged in vertical exploration (rearing) and locomoting, while susceptible rats were significantly more inactive during touchscreen testing sessions.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54 are supported by machine learning analysis (DeepLabCut and B-SOiD) with statistical significance (p-values provided) and data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A. The behavioral profiling provides mechanistic insight into differences between susceptible and resistant rats.

results.result: ABA-exposed but weight-recovered rats performed much worse than ABA-naïve rats on both discrimination and reversal learning tasks, an impairment that did not occur to the same extent in rats exposed to food restriction conditions alone. Half of ABA-exposed animals were unable to acquire the reversal learning task compared to 32% of food-restricted and 11% of ABA-naïve animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C13, C55-C58, C76, C83 collectively demonstrate persistent cognitive impairment following ABA exposure. The result is supported by multiple measures (acquisition rates, sessions to criterion, trial types) with appropriate statistical comparisons across three groups (ABA-exposed, food restriction-only, ABA-naïve) shown in Figures 4B-E. The specificity to ABA (not food restriction alone) strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: The number of correct, incorrect, and omitted trials to acquisition of initial discrimination were significantly greater in the ABA-exposed group, with learning impairment evident from the first session and even within the first 10 minutes of initial pairwise discrimination performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C59, C85 are supported by statistical analysis (p-values provided) and data in Figures 4D-E and Figure 4—figure supplement 5. The early emergence of impairment (first 10 minutes) suggests a fundamental deficit rather than a learning-specific problem.

results.result: During pairwise discrimination, ABA-exposed animals spent more time inactive and less time engaged in task-relevant behaviors (rotating, investigating, magazine interactions) than ABA-naïve animals, with behavioral profiles more similar between groups during reversal sessions.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 is supported by machine learning analysis of behavior (DeepLabCut and B-SOiD) with data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3. The differential behavioral profile during discrimination versus reversal provides insight into the nature of ABA-induced cognitive impairment.

results.result: Animals that had been trained on reversal learning were better able to resist weight loss upon subsequent exposure to the ABA model, losing significantly less body weight each day and eating more food when available. Operant training prior to ABA alters the subsequent development of anorectic phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C14, C61-C63, C81 demonstrate a protective effect of cognitive training against ABA. The result is supported by statistical analysis (p<0.0001 for resistance, p<0.0001 for daily weight loss, p=0.0009 for food intake) and data in Figures 5B-E. The dramatic increase in resistance rate (56% vs 5%) is compelling.

results.result: Rats that had undergone touchscreen testing prior to ABA showed a blunted hyperactive phenotype with significantly reduced overall running activity at baseline and during ABA, but showed elevated running specifically in the hour preceding food access (food anticipatory activity).
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 are supported by statistical analysis (multiple p-values <0.05) and data in Figures 5F-H. The differential effect on overall activity versus food anticipatory activity suggests a specific behavioral mechanism underlying the protective effect of cognitive training.

results.result: Machine learning tools (DeepLabCut and B-SOiD) uncovered stable behavioral differences between ABA susceptible versus resistant rats during touchscreen test sessions and enabled scoring of very large datasets (185 hours of footage).
results.evaluation: Claims C15, C90-C91 describe the methodological contribution of applying machine learning to behavioral analysis. The result is supported by data in supplementary figures and demonstrates the utility of these tools for hypothesis generation. The scale of analysis (185 hours) is impressive and validates the approach.

results.result: 55% of rats exposed to ABA conditions were able to maintain body weight above 80% of baseline throughout the 10 days of ABA, being classified as 'resistant'.
results.evaluation: Claim C50 reports the proportion of resistant rats (12/22, 55%) in the current study. This is a straightforward observational finding supported by the data, though the authors note this proportion is higher than typically observed and one cohort was surprisingly mostly susceptible (C82), suggesting some variability in the model.

results.result: The excessive exercise component of the ABA model disrupts the integration of new and existing learning necessary for reversal learning performance, pointing to a potential motivational deficit induced by ABA.
results.evaluation: Claims C77, C87 represent inferences from the finding that ABA but not food restriction impairs cognitive flexibility. While the data support differential effects of ABA versus food restriction (C76), the specific mechanism (disruption of learning integration, motivational deficit) is speculative. The impairment in both discrimination and reversal learning (C87) supports a broader deficit than flexibility alone, but the precise mechanism requires further investigation.

results.result: The cohort of rats that were experimentally naïve prior to ABA exposure was surprisingly mostly susceptible to weight loss (21/22 rats), a much higher proportion than is normally seen on a cohort-to-cohort basis.
results.evaluation: Claim C82 is an observation from the study's data. The authors acknowledge this is unusual and note it as a limitation. This high susceptibility rate in the control group strengthens the finding that cognitive training is protective (C14, C61), but also raises questions about cohort variability and whether this particular cohort was atypical.

results.result: Anorexia nervosa has among the highest mortality rates of any psychiatric disorder and is characterized by cognitive inflexibility that persists after weight recovery and contributes to the chronic nature of the condition.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 represent established knowledge about anorexia nervosa cited from the literature. While not original findings of this study, they provide essential context and are well-supported by the cited literature throughout the manuscript.

results.result: Previous work by the authors identified a neurobiological link between cognitive inflexibility and susceptibility to pathological weight loss in female rats using the ABA model, demonstrating that activity within a specific neural circuit (medial prefrontal cortex to nucleus accumbens shell) links pathological weight loss with cognitive inflexibility on reversal learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C73 describe prior work by the authors (Milton et al., 2021). These are appropriately cited and provide important context for the current study's hypothesis and findings. The current results (C10, C74) contradict the expected relationship, which is appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: Elevated food anticipatory activity is consistently associated with resistance to ABA in previous work by the authors.
results.evaluation: Claim C67 cites previous work by the authors (Milton et al., 2021; 2018; 2022) establishing the relationship between food anticipatory activity and ABA resistance. This provides context for interpreting the current finding (C66) that cognitive training increases food anticipatory activity.

results.result: The clinical presentation of inflexibility in patients with anorexia nervosa persists long after body weight recovery, which contrasts with the only other published report of flexible learning after ABA exposure where reversal learning impairment was ameliorated with weight recovery.
results.evaluation: Claims C84, C86 compare the current findings to clinical literature and prior animal studies. C84 is well-supported by multiple citations (Tchanturia et al., 2012; Friederich and Herzog, 2011; Tchanturia et al., 2004). C86 appropriately notes the discrepancy with Allen et al., 2017, though the reasons for this difference remain unclear.

results.result: Testing flexible learning prior to ABA exposure in the same animals has been impossible due to the length of training required and the necessity of daily handling, which can influence the development of ABA. Conventional touchscreen testing requires significant experimenter intervention, and experimenter involvement influences experimental outcomes, particularly for behavioral studies including the ABA model.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C30-C33 describe limitations of conventional approaches and provide rationale for the automated system. These are supported by citations (Carrera et al., 2006; Deutsch-Feldman et al., 2015; Sorge et al., 2014; Meijer et al., 2007) and represent established knowledge in the field.

results.result: Cognitive flexibility refers to the capacity to modify behavioral choices to meet changing environmental demands and is impaired across multiple psychiatric illnesses including schizophrenia, OCD, substance use disorders, and anorexia nervosa. In anorexia nervosa, impaired cognitive flexibility is most severe in acutely ill patients, likely contributes to perpetuating the condition, and persists after weight recovery in patients and unaffected sisters, suggesting involvement in the disorder's etiology.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C26 provide background on cognitive flexibility and its role in psychiatric disorders, particularly anorexia nervosa. These are well-supported by multiple citations and represent established knowledge that contextualizes the current study. The inference that persistence suggests etiological involvement (C23) is appropriately qualified as a suggestion.

results.result: The ABA model has been instrumental in identifying specific neural circuits that contribute to disordered cognitive functioning, and touchscreen testing in rodents closely mimics human cognitive testing, improving standardization and interpretation of data.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29 describe the rationale for using the ABA model and touchscreen testing. These are supported by citations (Milton et al., 2021; Bussey et al., 2008) and represent established methodological approaches in the field.

results.result: Social isolation can induce cognitive deficits and depression-like behavior, representing a confound for cognition assessment in rodent models, while appropriate social interaction can enhance neuroplasticity, emotional and social intelligence, and influence performance on complex cognitive tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C38 provide rationale for the social housing feature of the automated system. These are well-supported by multiple citations (Bianchi et al., 2006; Hemmer et al., 2019; Ieraci et al., 2016; Fone and Porkess, 2008; Liang et al., 2019; Torquet et al., 2018; Nagy et al., 2020) and represent established knowledge about social housing effects.

results.result: The learning rate of self-motivated and undisturbed rats was much faster when experimenter involvement is removed (Rivalan et al., 2017), and the ABA model develops differently in adult compared to adolescent ages.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40 cite prior work (Rivalan et al., 2017; Beeler and Burghardt, 2021) that provides rationale for the automated system and the importance of testing at appropriate ages. These are appropriately cited and contextualize the current study's approach.

results.result: Young female rats were used because they are particularly vulnerable to developing the ABA phenotype, which has translational relevance to the increased prevalence of anorexia nervosa in young women.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 describe the rationale for the study population. While the vulnerability of young female rats to ABA is stated as established knowledge, the translational relevance (C42) is appropriately qualified as an inference. This is a standard justification in the ABA literature.

results.result: A male rat was housed in experimental rooms to facilitate synchronization of cycling in female rats (Whitten Effect), because wheel running and food intake fluctuate with the estrous cycle in female rats.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44 describe a methodological approach to control for estrous cycle effects. This is supported by citations (Anantharaman-Barr and Decombaz, 1989; Cora et al., 2015) and represents an appropriate experimental control.

results.result: Rats exhibit increased activity and attention during the dark period.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 represent established knowledge about circadian activity patterns in rats, supported by citations (Milton et al., 2021; Bruinsma et al., 2019). This provides context for the dark-phase restriction findings (C48-C49, C70).

results.result: A loss of behavioral flexibility following disrupted cholinergic activity in the dorsal striatum was associated with facilitated habit formation and increased vulnerability to maladaptive eating in ABA mice, and only a subset of patients with anorexia nervosa show enhanced habit formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 cite prior work (Favier et al., 2020; Steding et al., 2019) that provides context for interpreting the current findings. These are appropriately cited and used to discuss the complexity of habit formation versus goal-directed behavior in anorexia nervosa.

results.result: Previous work demonstrated a role for the mesolimbic dopamine circuitry in the development and maintenance of the ABA phenotype, and exercise behavior in anorexia nervosa is linked with dopaminergic activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C89 cite prior work (Foldi et al., 2017; Gorrell et al., 2020) that provides mechanistic context for interpreting the motivational deficit suggested by the current findings (C87). These are appropriately cited and used to propose future directions.
